key_terms.meaning: A multiuser, multitasking operating system developed at Bell Labs in 1969, whose design ideas (files, processes, shell, small tools) Linux later copied.
A free, open source Unix-like kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991, now combined with GNU tools to form complete systems.
One machine can hold accounts for many people and serve several of them at the same time, each with separate files and permissions.
The kernel runs many processes apparently at once by switching the CPU between them quickly (time slicing).
A piece of kernel code that can be loaded or unloaded while the system runs, e.g. a device driver, without rebooting.
The privileged core program that owns memory, CPU time, devices and files, and is the only code that runs in kernel mode.
An ordinary user-space program that prints a prompt, reads your command line, and asks the kernel to run the program you named.
The part of memory where ordinary programs (shell, editor, browser) run with limited rights; they reach hardware only through system calls.
A controlled entry from a user program into the kernel, such as read(), write() or fork(), used to request a privileged service.
Software whose source code is published under a licence allowing anyone to study, modify and redistribute it.
The legal text that sets what you may do with the code; the GPL, for example, requires shared changes to stay under the same licence.
A ready-to-install bundle of the Linux kernel, libraries, shell and core utilities, installer, package manager and extra software.
A tool such as apt or dnf that downloads, installs, upgrades and removes software packages and tracks their dependencies.
The program that partitions the disk, copies the system, sets up the bootloader and creates your first user account.
The first user-space process (PID 1) started by the kernel at boot; it starts and supervises all other services.
A Debian-based distribution from Canonical, popular for beginners and desktops, using apt and .deb packages.
A long-lived, community-run distribution that Ubuntu and many others are built from; known for stability and strict free-software rules.
Red Hat Enterprise Linux, a commercially supported distribution using dnf and .rpm packages; Fedora is its fast-moving upstream.
The short text the shell prints when it is ready for a command, often showing user, host and current directory, ending in $ or #.
The directory you are standing in; a bare filename in a command is resolved against it (shown by pwd).

takeaways: Unix gave the model (files, processes, shell, small tools); Linux gave a free, open implementation of that model.
Multi-user, multitasking and modularity are kernel-level promises, not extra features bolted on top.
The kernel is the only privileged code; the shell is just another user-space program that asks the kernel for work.
Open source lowers lock-in and spreads the cost of finding and fixing bugs across many users.
A distribution is kernel plus libraries, tools, installer and package manager; the distro choice mostly decides your package manager and support model.
Installation means answering four questions: where to install, how to boot it, which user accounts, and which packages.
The command line is a loop: prompt, read, run, return; every basic command is a small program in that loop.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to trace Unix/Linux history and then explain the kernel-shell-user-space split and the distribution and command-line layers, so prepare a layered diagram you can redraw and label.

bank.q: Trace the origin of Unix at Bell Labs and the origin of Linux in 1991. Explain how the two projects differ in goals, licensing and how they are shipped to users today.
outline: Unix: 1969, Bell Labs, multiuser time-sharing system, later commercial and closed variants
Linux: 1991, Linus Torvalds, kernel only, released under GPL, combined with GNU tools
Unix = a whole commercial OS; Linux = a free kernel plus distributions
Today's systems follow Unix design but use the Linux kernel

bank.q: Explain the Linux features multi-user, multitasking and modularity. Give one concrete example of each.
outline: Multi-user: accounts, ownership, permissions, one server many logins
Multitasking: scheduler, time slices, foreground/background jobs
Modularity: loadable kernel modules, insmod/modprobe, device drivers
Examples: college server with many logins, music player while compiling, Wi-Fi driver loaded on demand

bank.q: Distinguish the kernel, the shell and user space. Describe step by step what happens after you type ls and press Enter.
outline: Kernel: privileged, memory/CPU/device/file control
User space: restricted memory region for ordinary programs
Shell: user-space program, reads line, parses, forks and execs
System call boundary: fork, exec, read directory, write to terminal
Shell prints prompt again when child exits

bank.q: Define open source software and state its benefits. Mention the role of the licence with one example licence.
outline: Source code available, right to study, modify, redistribute
Benefits: no vendor lock-in, auditability, community bug fixing, low cost, long life after vendor exits
Licence sets the rules; GPL requires derivatives to stay open
Contrast with closed binary-only software

bank.q: What is a Linux distribution? List its components and name four widely used distributions with the package manager each uses.
outline: Kernel + libraries + shell and core utilities + installer + package manager + extra software
Ubuntu/Debian: apt; Fedora/RHEL: dnf; SUSE: zypper; Arch: pacman
Community vs commercially supported distros

bank.q: Given a directory tree, write the commands to create a project folder, move into it, list all files including hidden ones in long format, copy a file, rename it, and delete an empty folder. Show the output you expect.
outline: mkdir project; cd project; pwd to confirm
ls -la for hidden and long listing
cp source dest; mv old new
rmdir for empty directory, rm for files
Relative vs absolute path used in each command

bank.q: Explain the ls command with the options -l, -a, -h, -t and -R. Show sample output lines and say what each column means.
outline: -l long listing: permissions, links, owner, group, size, date, name
-a shows dot files; -h human-readable sizes; -t sort by modification time; -R recursive
Interpret the permission string and the total line

bank.q: Compare cat, more and less for viewing files. Give the situation where each is the right tool and write the commands.
outline: cat: short files, concatenation, redirection
more: page-by-page forward only
less: forward and backward, search with /, does not load whole file
Practical rule for large log files

bank.q: Explain find, cp, mv, rm and ln with syntax and one useful example each, including how to copy a whole directory tree and how a hard link differs from a symbolic link.
outline: find path -name pattern -type f
cp -r for directories, -i to avoid overwrite
mv for rename and move across directories
rm -i, rm -r; no recycle bin
ln file hard; ln -s file soft link; inode difference

bank.q: A student has an old laptop with 4 GB RAM, a college lab needs a server, and a hobbyist wants the newest software. Recommend a distribution and an installation option for each, with reasons.
outline: Lightweight desktop or minimal install for old laptop
Stable server distro with LTS support for the lab
Rolling-release distro for newest software
Dual boot vs full disk vs virtual machine vs live USB
Mention installer steps: partitioning, bootloader, user, packages

bank.q: Analyse the claim that open source makes software more secure. Support and oppose it using the ideas of modularity, licence obligations and the many-eyes argument, and state your conclusion.
outline: Many readers can find bugs; patches move fast
But not all code is read; modules can be binary-only
GPL forces shared fixes; permissive licences may not
Security also depends on configuration and update discipline
Balanced conclusion, not a slogan

bank.q: A newly installed machine stops at a black screen with no prompt. Break the boot path into stages (firmware, bootloader, kernel, init, login shell) and explain how you would test each stage to locate the fault.
outline: Firmware/POST, bootloader menu, kernel messages, init starting services, getty/login, shell startup files
Test by booting from live USB, checking logs, using single-user or rescue mode
Distinguish kernel failure from shell or login failure
Prevention: keep a live USB and know the recovery entry

bank.q: Compare the command line with a graphical desktop for system administration. Evaluate which is better for repeatable work, remote access and learning, and justify your answer with examples.
outline: Command line: scriptable, remote over ssh, low bandwidth, exact
GUI: discoverable, good for media and browsing
Repetition: shell scripts and history beat clicking
Learning: commands reveal the kernel-shell model
Recommendation: both, command line for admin

glossary.def: A multiuser, multitasking operating system built at Bell Labs from 1969 whose design Linux follows.
The free, open source kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991 and used in distributions such as Ubuntu and Fedora.
The privileged core of the system that controls memory, CPU time, devices and files.
A user-space program that reads commands from you and asks the kernel to execute them.
The restricted memory area where ordinary programs run and reach hardware only through system calls.
A defined request from a user program to the kernel, such as read, write or fork.
A running program together with its memory, registers and open files, identified by a PID.
A property of the system that lets many people have accounts and work on one machine at once.
Running many processes apparently at the same time by switching the CPU between them.
A loadable piece of kernel code, often a device driver, added or removed without rebooting.
Software released with its source code under a licence that permits study, change and redistribution.
The GNU General Public License, which requires modified versions of the code to stay under the same licence.
A complete installable system made of the Linux kernel, libraries, utilities, installer and package manager.
A program such as apt, dnf, zypper or pacman that installs, upgrades and removes software and tracks dependencies.
Process number 1, started by the kernel at boot, which brings up and supervises all other services.
The small program that loads the kernel into memory and hands control to it at startup.
A bootable USB stick that runs a full distribution in memory without installing it, useful for testing and repair.
The graphical layer (windows, panels, menus) that runs on top of the kernel and shell, e.g. GNOME or KDE.
The window or device that connects you to a shell so you can type commands.
The shell's short ready signal, often user@host:dir$ , printed before it reads a command.
The directory you are currently in, printed by pwd and used to resolve relative paths.
A path starting at the root /, such as /home/ravi/notes.txt, valid from any directory.
A path interpreted from the current working directory, such as ../notes.txt.
The built-in reference page for a command, opened with man command or read with --help.
